title: Lab 6 review: the respiratory system
summary: The airway from nostril to alveolus, the lungs and pleurae, and how a breath is moved and measured.
objectives: Trace air from the nose to the alveoli and say where the conducting zone ends
Identify the laryngeal cartilages, the trachea, the main bronchi and the lobes of each lung
Name the cells of the alveolus and the layers of the respiratory membrane
Explain inspiration with Boyle's law and add up lung volumes into capacities
takeaways: The conducting zone ends at the terminal bronchioles; gas exchange starts at the respiratory bronchioles.
Cricoid = the only complete cartilage ring; epiglottis = elastic cartilage.
Right main bronchus: wider, shorter, more vertical. Right lung 3 lobes, left lung 2 plus the cardiac notch.
Type II pneumocytes make surfactant; macrophages clean the alveoli.
VC = TV + IRV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV; minute ventilation = TV × rate.

steps.title: Nose to bronchioles: the conducting zone
steps.text:
Air follows a fixed route: nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → main bronchi → lobar and segmental bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles. All of this is the conducting zone: it filters, warms and moistens the air but exchanges no gas.

The respiratory zone begins at the respiratory bronchioles and continues into alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli. In the nose, the conchae churn the air so its mucus can catch dust.

check.q: Where does the conducting zone end and the respiratory zone begin?
check.a: It ends at the terminal bronchioles; the respiratory zone starts with the respiratory bronchioles.

steps.title: The larynx: cartilages and folds
steps.text:
The larynx is a box of cartilage. The big thyroid cartilage forms the Adam's apple; below it the cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring; the small paired arytenoid and corniculate cartilages sit at the back and move the vocal folds. The leaf-shaped epiglottis, made of elastic cartilage, tips over the inlet during swallowing.

The upper vestibular (false) folds make no sound; the lower vocal (true) folds vibrate, and the gap between them is the glottis.

check.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is a complete ring, and which one is elastic cartilage?
check.a: The cricoid is the complete ring; the epiglottis is elastic cartilage.

steps.title: Trachea and bronchial tree
steps.text:
The trachea is kept open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage; the open back of each C faces the oesophagus and is bridged by the trachealis smooth muscle. Its lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells: mucus traps particles and the cilia sweep them up to the pharynx.

At the carina the trachea splits. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled objects usually lodge on the right.

check.q: Why does an inhaled peanut usually end up in the right lung?
check.a: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

steps.title: Lungs and pleurae
steps.text:
The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) and two fissures, oblique and horizontal. The left lung has two lobes and one oblique fissure, and its cardiac notch and tongue-like lingula make room for the heart.

Each lung sits in a double sac of pleura: visceral pleura on the lung, parietal pleura lining the chest wall, and a film of serous fluid in the pleural cavity between them that lets them glide while holding the lung to the wall.

check.q: How many lobes and fissures does each lung have?
check.a: Right: three lobes, two fissures (oblique and horizontal). Left: two lobes, one oblique fissure.

steps.title: Alveoli and the respiratory membrane
steps.text:
Most of the alveolar wall is type I pneumocytes: very thin simple squamous cells. Rounder type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse. Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) eat whatever gets past the cilia.

Gas crosses the respiratory membrane: type I cell, fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium, well under a micrometre thick. Oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide out, each down its partial-pressure gradient.

check.q: What do type II pneumocytes secrete, and why does it matter?
check.a: Surfactant; it lowers surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse.

steps.title: A breath, measured
steps.text:
By Boyle's law, pressure and volume vary inversely. In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs; the chest grows, intrapulmonary pressure drops below atmospheric and air flows in. Quiet expiration is passive recoil.

Tidal volume is about 500 mL. VC = TV + IRV + ERV and TLC = VC + RV; the residual volume can never be blown out. Minute ventilation = TV × breaths per minute.

check.q: TV 500 mL, IRV 3000 mL, ERV 1200 mL, RV 1200 mL. What are VC and TLC?
check.a: VC = 4700 mL; TLC = 5900 mL.

practice.q: Put the airway in order, from outside in
Which muscles contract in a quiet inspiration?
practice.why: Quiet inspiration is active (diaphragm + external intercostals); quiet expiration is passive recoil.

practice.q: The residual volume is included in which of these?
practice.why: TLC = VC + RV; the residual volume can never be exhaled, so it is not part of VC.

practice.q: Breathing 12 times a minute with a 500 mL tidal volume: what is the minute ventilation?

title: Lab 7 review: lung function and fitness
summary: FEV1 and vital capacity, obstructive versus restrictive disease, and the numbers behind fitness tests.
objectives: Define VC, FEV1 and FEV1/VC% and give the normal ratio
Tell an obstructive from a restrictive pattern and name causes of each
Calculate a personal fitness index, a target heart rate zone, a BMI and a waist-to-hip ratio
takeaways: FEV1/VC% is normally about 75% or more.
Obstructive: ratio low, VC normal. Restrictive: VC low, ratio normal.
PFI = seconds × 100 ÷ (2 × sum of the three recovery counts).
MHR ≈ 220 − age; target zone 60–80% of it. BMI = kg ÷ m².

steps.title: VC, FEV1 and the ratio
steps.text:
Vital capacity (VC) is the most air you can breathe out after the deepest possible breath in. FEV1 is how much of it leaves in the first second of a hard, fast exhalation. Their ratio, FEV1/VC%, is normally about 75% or more.

On a spirogram, which plots volume against time, VC is the peak-to-peak height of the forced breath, and FEV1 is read one second after the exhalation starts.

check.q: FEV1 is 3.0 L and VC is 5.0 L. What is the ratio, and is it normal?
check.a: 60%: low (normal is about 75% or more), which points to obstruction.

steps.title: Obstructive or restrictive?
steps.text:
Obstructive disease narrows the airways (asthma, bronchitis, excess mucus, emphysema), so air leaves slowly: FEV1/VC% falls while VC can stay normal. Most COPD comes from smoking; graded by the ratio, 60–74% is mild, 50–59% moderate and under 50% severe.

Restrictive disease stops the lungs filling: fibrosis (asbestosis, silicosis), pleural adhesions, lung resection, or a diaphragm paralysed by phrenic nerve damage. VC falls but the ratio stays normal.

check.q: Which value is low in each pattern?
check.a: Obstructive: FEV1/VC% is low. Restrictive: VC is low with a normal ratio.

steps.title: Heart rate and the step test
steps.text:
Aerobically trained people have a lower resting heart rate, and their rate recovers faster after exercise. Stop at once for chest pain, pain spreading down the left arm (angina) or faintness.

In the Harvard step test you step 30 times a minute for up to five minutes, then count the pulse for 30 s at 1, 2 and 3 minutes of recovery. PFI = seconds of exercise × 100 ÷ (2 × sum of the three counts). Under 55 is poor, 80–89 good, 90 or more excellent.

check.q: 300 s of stepping, recovery counts 70, 60 and 50. What is the PFI?

steps.title: Cooper run, target zone, BMI and WHR
steps.text:
The Cooper test rates aerobic fitness by the distance covered in 12 minutes; under age 40, over 2700 m is excellent. Maximum heart rate ≈ 220 − age, and the target zone is 60–80% of it.

BMI = kg ÷ m²: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5–24.9 normal, 25–29.9 overweight, 30 or more obese; it overrates fat in muscular people. Waist-to-hip ratio (waist just above the umbilicus ÷ widest hips) flags risky central fat: high above 0.85 in women and 1.0 in men.

check.q: What is the target heart rate zone of a 40-year-old?
check.a: MHR ≈ 180 bpm, so the zone is 108–144 bpm.

practice.q: A patient has a normal VC and an FEV1/VC% of 55%. The pattern is:
practice.why: A low ratio with a normal VC is obstruction; 50–59% is moderate.

practice.q: Which of these causes a restrictive pattern?
choices: Phrenic nerve damage paralysing the diaphragm
practice.why: A paralysed diaphragm cannot fill the lungs, so VC falls; the others narrow the airways.

practice.q: A BMI of 27 is classed as:
practice.why: 25–29.9 is overweight.

practice.q: A woman's waist-to-hip ratio is 0.90. Her risk is:
practice.why: For women, above 0.85 is high risk (0.81–0.85 moderate).

practice.q: Give the formula for the Harvard step test personal fitness index.
practice.a: PFI = duration of exercise in seconds × 100 ÷ (2 × sum of the three 30-second recovery pulse counts).

practice.q: Why is a lower resting heart rate a sign of aerobic fitness?
practice.a: A trained heart pumps a larger stroke volume, so it needs fewer beats to move the same output, and it also returns to resting faster after exercise.

title: Lab 8 review: the digestive system
summary: The gut wall, the mouth and teeth, stomach, intestines, liver and pancreas: the facts a practical asks.
objectives: Name the four tunics of the gut wall and the two nerve plexuses
Identify the teeth, salivary glands and muscles of mastication and give the dental formulas
Identify the regions of the stomach, small and large intestine and the cells or features that mark each
Describe the liver lobule and trace bile to the duodenum
takeaways: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa (adventitia on the oesophagus).
Adult 2-1-2-3 = 32 teeth; child 2-1-0-2 = 20.
Stomach adds an inner oblique layer; parietal cells make HCl, chief cells pepsinogen.
Brunner glands = duodenum; Peyer patches = ileum; taeniae, haustra and fat tags = colon.
Portal triad = portal venule, hepatic arteriole, bile ductule.

steps.title: The tube and its four layers
steps.text:
The alimentary canal runs mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus; teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas are the accessory organs.

From the lumen out, the wall has four tunics: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa (with the submucosal plexus), muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal, the myenteric plexus between them) and serosa, or adventitia where there is no peritoneum.

check.q: Name the four tunics of the gut wall from the lumen outward.
check.a: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa (or adventitia).

steps.title: Mouth, teeth and salivary glands
steps.text:
A tooth has an enamel crown, a neck at the gum line and a root coated in cementum and slung by the periodontal ligament; dentin surrounds the pulp. Adults have 32 teeth (per quadrant 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars); children have 20 (2-1-0-2).

The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar; the submandibular and sublingual glands open under the tongue. Chewing: masseter, temporalis and the two pterygoids.

check.q: Write the adult and the deciduous dental formula.
check.a: Adult 2-1-2-3 per quadrant (32 teeth); deciduous 2-1-0-2 (20 teeth).

steps.title: Oesophagus and stomach
steps.text:
The oesophagus has a stratified squamous lining and skeletal muscle above, smooth below; it pierces the diaphragm to reach the cardia. The stomach continues as fundus, body and pyloric part, ending at the pyloric sphincter, with greater and lesser curvatures and rugae when empty.

Its muscularis adds an inner oblique layer for churning. Gastric glands hold parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen) beneath a surface of mucous cells.

check.q: Which gastric cells make HCl and which make pepsinogen?
check.a: Parietal cells make HCl (and intrinsic factor); chief cells make pepsinogen.

steps.title: Small intestine
steps.text:
Three parts: the C-shaped duodenum (about 25 cm; bile and pancreatic juice enter at the major duodenal papilla), the jejunum and the ileum, which ends at the ileocaecal valve. Circular folds, villi and microvilli multiply the absorbing surface.

Each villus holds capillaries and a central lacteal that takes up fat. On a slide, Brunner glands in the submucosa mean duodenum, and Peyer patches mean ileum.

check.q: Which feature marks the duodenum on a slide, and which marks the ileum?
check.a: Brunner (duodenal) glands in the submucosa; Peyer patches in the ileum.

steps.title: Large intestine
steps.text:
From the caecum, which carries the vermiform appendix, the colon runs ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid, then the rectum and anal canal. Its longitudinal muscle is gathered into three taeniae coli, which pucker the wall into haustra, and fat tags (epiploic appendices) hang from it.

The mucosa has no villi, just straight crypts packed with goblet cells. The internal anal sphincter is smooth and involuntary; the external is skeletal and voluntary.

check.q: Name three surface features that tell colon from small intestine.
check.a: Taeniae coli, haustra and epiploic appendices (fat tags).

steps.title: Liver, bile and pancreas
steps.text:
The liver has right, left, quadrate and caudate lobes; the portal vein and hepatic artery enter, and bile leaves, at the porta hepatis. A lobule is a hexagon of hepatocyte plates around a central vein, with portal triads at its corners and Kupffer cells in the sinusoids.

Bile: hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct, joined by the cystic duct → common bile duct → hepatopancreatic ampulla → duodenum. The pancreas is exocrine acini around endocrine islets.

check.q: What three vessels make up a portal triad?
check.a: A branch of the hepatic portal vein, a branch of the hepatic artery and a bile ductule.

practice.q: Put bile's route from the liver in order
Which layer of the tooth is the hardest and covers the crown?
practice.why: Enamel caps the crown; cementum covers the root.

title: Lab 8 review: the urinary system
summary: The kidney from its wrappings to the nephron, how blood and filtrate flow, and the tubes that carry urine out.
objectives: Describe where the kidneys lie and name their three coverings
Identify cortex, pyramids, columns, papillae, calyces and pelvis
Trace blood through the kidney and filtrate through the nephron
Describe the bladder wall, its epithelium and the two urethral sphincters
takeaways: Kidneys are retroperitoneal, about T12–L3, right slightly lower.
Papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter.
Afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries / vasa recta.
Filtration, reabsorption, secretion. Transitional epithelium lines the bladder.

steps.title: The kidneys in place
steps.text:
The kidneys are retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall, roughly T12–L3, the right a little lower because of the liver; a suprarenal gland caps each. Three wrappings, inside out: fibrous capsule, perirenal fat and renal fascia, which anchors it.

At the medial hilum the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave. The left renal vein is the longer, crossing in front of the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava.

check.q: List the three coverings of the kidney from the inside out.
check.a: Fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat (adipose capsule), renal fascia.

steps.title: Inside the kidney
steps.text: A frontal cut shows the outer cortex and the inner medulla, built of cone-shaped renal pyramids separated by renal columns of cortex-like tissue. The tip of each pyramid, the papilla, drips urine into a minor calyx. Minor calyces join into major calyces, which merge into the funnel of the renal pelvis, and that narrows into the ureter. The fat-filled space around them is the renal sinus.

check.q: Trace urine from a renal papilla to the ureter.
check.a: Papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter.

steps.title: Blood through the kidney
steps.text:
Renal artery → segmental → interlobar (running in the columns) → arcuate (arching over the pyramid bases) → cortical radiate → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries or vasa recta. The veins return in reverse: cortical radiate, arcuate, interlobar, renal vein.

That is two capillary beds in a row: the glomerulus filters at high pressure, the peritubular bed reabsorbs at low pressure.

check.q: Which vessel carries blood out of the glomerulus?
check.a: The efferent arteriole, which feeds the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta.

steps.title: The nephron and urine formation
steps.text:
Filtrate path: glomerular (Bowman) capsule → proximal convoluted tubule (cuboidal cells with a brush border; most reabsorption) → nephron loop → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct. Glomerulus plus capsule is the renal corpuscle; podocytes wrap its capillaries.

Urine forms by filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion. Where the distal tubule meets the afferent arteriole, the macula densa and renin-making juxtaglomerular cells form the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

check.q: Name the three processes that form urine.
check.a: Glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion.

steps.title: Ureters, bladder and urethra
steps.text:
The ureters carry urine by peristalsis and enter the bladder obliquely, so a full bladder presses them shut. The bladder's smooth muscle is the detrusor; its lining is transitional epithelium, whose dome-shaped umbrella cells flatten as it stretches. The trigone lies between the two ureteric openings and the urethra.

The internal urethral sphincter is smooth and involuntary, the external skeletal and voluntary. The female urethra is about 4 cm; the male's, about 20 cm, is prostatic, membranous and spongy.

check.q: Which epithelium lines the bladder, and why does it suit it?
check.a: Transitional epithelium (urothelium): its surface cells flatten as the bladder fills, so it stretches without tearing and stays waterproof.

practice.q: Put the arteries of the kidney in order
Most reabsorption of filtrate happens in the:
practice.why: Its brush border gives the proximal tubule a huge surface; it reclaims about two-thirds of the filtrate.

practice.q: Which sphincter is under voluntary control?
practice.why: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle; the internal one is smooth muscle at the bladder neck.

title: Lab 9 review: the male reproductive system
summary: Testis, sperm production, the duct system, the glands that make semen, and the penis and perineum.
objectives: Describe the coverings of the testis and how the scrotum keeps it cool
Order the cells of spermatogenesis and name the Sertoli and Leydig cells' jobs
Trace a sperm from the seminiferous tubule to the exterior and say what each gland adds
Identify the three erectile bodies and the two triangles of the perineum
takeaways: Spermatogonia → primary spermatocytes → secondary spermatocytes → spermatids → sperm.
Leydig cells make testosterone; Sertoli cells nurse the germ cells.
Epididymis → ductus deferens → ejaculatory duct → prostatic, membranous, spongy urethra.
Seminal glands give most of the semen; the corpus spongiosum carries the urethra.

steps.title: Scrotum and testis
steps.text:
The testes hang in the scrotum, about 3 °C below core temperature. The dartos wrinkles the skin, the cremaster pulls the testis up, and the pampiniform plexus of veins cools the incoming arterial blood.

Each testis is wrapped in the serous tunica vaginalis and the tough tunica albuginea, whose septa divide it into lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules. These drain through the rete testis and efferent ductules into the epididymis.

check.q: Give two ways the testes are kept cooler than the body.
check.a: Hanging in the scrotum, the dartos and cremaster adjusting their distance from the body, and the pampiniform plexus cooling the arterial blood.

steps.title: Making sperm
steps.text:
Spermatogenesis runs from the tubule wall inward to the lumen: spermatogonia (2n, dividing by mitosis) → primary spermatocytes (2n, entering meiosis I) → secondary spermatocytes (n, meiosis II) → spermatids (n) → spermatozoa. Remodelling a round spermatid into a sperm is spermiogenesis.

Sertoli cells nurse the germ cells and form the blood–testis barrier; Leydig (interstitial) cells between the tubules make testosterone in response to LH.

check.q: Which cells make testosterone, and where are they?
check.a: Leydig (interstitial) cells, in the connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules.

steps.title: The sperm cell
steps.text:
A sperm has three parts. The head holds the haploid nucleus under the acrosome, a cap of enzymes that digests a path through the egg's coverings. The midpiece is wrapped in a spiral of mitochondria that supply the energy. The tail, a flagellum, drives it forward.

Sperm leave the testis unable to swim; they mature and are stored in the epididymis.

check.q: What is in the acrosome, and what is in the midpiece?
check.a: The acrosome holds digestive enzymes for penetrating the egg; the midpiece holds mitochondria that power the tail.

steps.title: Ducts and glands
steps.text:
From the testis sperm pass through the epididymis (head, body, tail) into the ductus deferens. It climbs in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, crosses over the ureter behind the bladder, widens into its ampulla, and joins the seminal gland's duct as the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra.

Semen: seminal glands about 60% (alkaline, fructose), prostate about 30% (milky, with clotting enzymes), and the bulbourethral glands a little clear mucus first.

check.q: What does the spermatic cord contain?
check.a: The ductus deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform venous plexus, nerves and lymphatics, wrapped in the spermatic fasciae and cremaster.

steps.title: Penis, urethra and perineum
steps.text:
The penis has three erectile bodies: two dorsal corpora cavernosa and a ventral corpus spongiosum, which carries the spongy urethra and swells into the glans under the prepuce. The male urethra runs prostatic → membranous → spongy.

The diamond-shaped perineum, bounded by the pubic symphysis, the ischial tuberosities and the coccyx, divides into a front urogenital triangle and a back anal triangle.

check.q: Which erectile body carries the urethra?
check.a: The corpus spongiosum, which ends as the glans.

practice.q: Put the cells of spermatogenesis in order
Which gland contributes the largest share of semen?
practice.why: The seminal glands give about 60% of the volume, rich in fructose.

practice.q: The first cells in spermatogenesis to be haploid are the:
practice.why: Meiosis I halves the chromosome number, so the secondary spermatocytes it produces are n.

title: Lab 9 review: the female system and early development
summary: Ovary and follicles, the tract and its ligaments, the two cycles, the breast, and the first weeks after fertilisation.
objectives: Order the stages of follicle development and oogenesis
Identify the parts of the uterine tube, uterus and vagina and the layers of the uterine wall
Name the parts of the broad ligament and the other ligaments of the ovary and uterus
Match the phases of the ovarian and uterine cycles to their hormones
Trace development from zygote to blastocyst and name the germ-layer derivatives
takeaways: Primordial → primary → secondary → vesicular follicle → ovulation → corpus luteum → corpus albicans.
Fertilisation happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
The LH surge triggers ovulation; the corpus luteum makes progesterone.
The functional layer of the endometrium is shed; the basal layer regrows it.
Ectoderm: skin and nervous system. Mesoderm: muscle, bone, blood, kidney. Endoderm: gut and lung linings.

steps.title: Ovary and oogenesis
steps.text:
Before birth, oogonia become primary oocytes that pause in prophase I inside primordial follicles. Each cycle a few grow into primary follicles, then secondary follicles with a fluid-filled antrum; one becomes the mature vesicular (Graafian) follicle, its oocyte on a cumulus oophorus.

Meiosis I ends just before ovulation, giving a secondary oocyte and a polar body; meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters. The empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, then the white scar of the corpus albicans.

check.q: At what stage is the oocyte released at ovulation, and when does it finish meiosis?
check.a: As a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II; it finishes meiosis II only if fertilised.

steps.title: Tube, uterus and vagina
steps.text:
The uterine tube runs from the finger-like fimbriae and funnel of the infundibulum, through the wide ampulla, the usual site of fertilisation, and the narrow isthmus into the uterus. The uterus has a fundus, body, isthmus and cervix, which opens into the vagina at the external os; the vaginal recess around it is the fornix.

The uterine wall: endometrium (a functional layer that is shed over a basal layer that regrows it), muscular myometrium, and outer perimetrium.

check.q: Which layer of the endometrium is shed at menstruation?
check.a: The stratum functionalis; the stratum basalis stays and regenerates it.

steps.title: Ligaments and the vulva
steps.text:
The broad ligament is a sheet of peritoneum in three parts: mesometrium beside the uterus, mesosalpinx under the tube and mesovarium holding the ovary. The ovarian ligament ties the ovary to the uterus; the suspensory ligament ties it to the pelvic wall and carries the ovarian vessels; the round ligament runs through the inguinal canal to the labia majora.

The vulva: mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris, and the vestibule with the urethral and vaginal openings and the greater vestibular glands.

check.q: Which ligament carries the ovarian artery and vein?
check.a: The suspensory ligament of the ovary.

steps.title: Two cycles, one clock
steps.text: Hypothalamic GnRH makes the anterior pituitary release FSH and LH. Ovary: in the follicular phase FSH grows follicles that make oestrogen; an LH surge triggers ovulation around day 14; in the luteal phase the corpus luteum makes progesterone. Uterus: menstrual (days 1–5), proliferative (oestrogen rebuilds the lining), secretory (progesterone readies it). Without pregnancy the corpus luteum dies and progesterone falls. The pill works by suppressing FSH and LH, so there is no ovulation.

check.q: Which hormone triggers ovulation, and which structure then makes progesterone?
check.a: The LH surge; the corpus luteum.

steps.title: The breast
steps.text: Each breast holds 15-20 lobes of gland set in fat. Each lobe's lobules of milk-making alveoli drain into a lactiferous duct, which opens on the nipple, inside the pigmented areola. The lactiferous sinus is a traditional subareolar label: Ramsay et al. (2005) found branching ducts without classical sac-like sinuses in ultrasound scans of 21 lactating women. Suspensory (Cooper) ligaments tie the skin to the fascia over pectoralis major. The alveoli develop fully only in pregnancy and lactation.

check.q: Trace milk from where it is made to the nipple.
check.a: Alveoli of a lobule â†’ lactiferous ducts â†’ openings on the nipple. The traditional lactiferous-sinus label identifies the subareolar region; a distinct storage sac was not observed in Ramsay et al.'s lactating-ultrasound study.

steps.title: Fertilisation to germ layers
steps.text:
Sperm meet the egg in the ampulla; the acrosome clears a path, the egg finishes meiosis II and the pronuclei join as a zygote. Cleavage gives 2, 4, 8 cells, then a solid morula, then a hollow blastocyst: outer trophoblast (future placenta) and inner cell mass (future embryo). It implants about day 7.

Germ layers: ectoderm (epidermis, nervous system), mesoderm (muscle, bone, blood, kidneys), endoderm (gut and airway linings, liver, pancreas).

check.q: Which part of the blastocyst becomes the embryo, and which helps form the placenta?
check.a: The inner cell mass becomes the embryo; the trophoblast forms the chorion and fetal placenta.

practice.q: Put the stages of follicle development in order
Put early development in order
Which germ layer gives rise to the nervous system?
practice.why: Ectoderm makes the epidermis and the whole nervous system.

practice.q: During the secretory phase of the uterine cycle the dominant hormone is:
practice.why: The secretory phase matches the luteal phase: the corpus luteum's progesterone makes the glands secrete.

title: Practice exam: Labs 6–9
summary: A mixed practical drawing on every question from Labs 6–9, plus routes and comparisons that cut across them.
objectives: Find and name the structures of the respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems
Trace air, food, filtrate, urine, sperm and the oocyte along their routes
Compare the epithelia and walls of organs across systems
takeaways: Missed items come back in Review what is due; retry the missed ones before the practical.
Routes and epithelia link the four labs: know both for every organ.

practice.q: Inhaled oxygen: put the route from nostril to red cell in order
A swallowed bolus: put the route in order
Undigested residue: put the large intestine in order
Filtrate becoming urine: put the route in order
A sperm: put its route from where it is made to the exterior in order
An oocyte and embryo: put the route from ovary to implantation in order
Oxygen crossing from the alveolus: put the layers in order
Which organ is lined by transitional epithelium?
practice.why: Urothelium lines the renal pelvis, ureters and bladder; it stretches as they fill.

practice.q: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the:
practice.why: The mucociliary lining of the conducting airways.

practice.q: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium lines both the oesophagus and the:
practice.why: Both surfaces take abrasion, so both have a many-layered squamous lining.

practice.q: Simple squamous epithelium forms both the alveolar wall and the:
choices: Parietal layer of the glomerular capsule
practice.why: Type I pneumocytes and the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule are both thin squamous cells.

practice.q: A brush border of microvilli is found on enterocytes and on the cells of the:
practice.why: Both are built for absorption; microvilli multiply the surface.

practice.q: Ciliated simple columnar epithelium that moves an egg lines the:
practice.why: The cilia beat toward the uterus, helped by peristalsis.

practice.q: Which passage is shared by air and food?
practice.why: The oropharynx and laryngopharynx carry both; the nasopharynx is air only.

practice.q: Which tube carries both urine and semen?
practice.why: The ejaculatory ducts open into the prostatic urethra, which also drains the bladder.

practice.q: Which of these is retroperitoneal?
practice.why: The kidneys, most of the duodenum and pancreas, and the ascending and descending colon lie behind the peritoneum.

practice.q: Which pair of sphincters are both smooth muscle and involuntary?
practice.why: The internal sphincters are smooth muscle; the external ones are skeletal and voluntary.

practice.q: Which two organs have an extra third layer of smooth muscle in their wall?
practice.why: The stomach adds an inner oblique layer; the detrusor is arranged in three layers.

practice.q: Near the bladder, which structure crosses over the ureter in a male?
practice.why: The ductus deferens passes over the ureter on its way behind the bladder.

practice.q: Which set of cells makes no digestive enzymes?
choices: Chief cells, acinar cells, parietal cells
Chief cells, Leydig cells, goblet cells
Acinar cells, type II pneumocytes, chief cells
Type II pneumocytes, parietal cells, Leydig cells
practice.why: Surfactant, HCl and testosterone; chief and acinar cells make enzymes.

practice.q: Match each secretion to its cell: surfactant, HCl, pepsinogen, testosterone, renin.
practice.a: Type II pneumocyte; parietal cell; chief cell; Leydig cell; juxtaglomerular cell.

practice.q: Name three places where two capillary beds (or a capillary bed and sinusoids) sit in series.
practice.a: The kidney (glomerulus then peritubular capillaries), the liver (gut capillaries → hepatic portal vein → sinusoids) and the pituitary (hypothalamic capillaries → portal veins → anterior pituitary capillaries).

practice.q: Where are cilia, stereocilia and microvilli found in Labs 6–9?
practice.a: Cilia: airway lining and the uterine tube. Stereocilia: the epididymis. Microvilli: small-intestine enterocytes and the proximal convoluted tubule.

practice.q: Compare meiosis in the testis and the ovary.
practice.a: The testis makes four sperm from each primary spermatocyte, continuously from puberty. The ovary makes one egg plus polar bodies, starts before birth, pauses in prophase I and finishes meiosis II only at fertilisation.
